Rainfall, Block by Block

Every volunteer in the Brookfield Rain Network record[1] precipitation from a small gauge mounted near home. The volunteers—students, gardeners, bus drivers, and retirees,[2] read their gauges at the same time each morning and submit the totals through a shared form. Because a storm can release different amounts of rain only a few streets apart, the combined readings create a more detailed neighborhood picture than one distant instrument can provide.

During training, participants learn to place gauges away from roofs and trees, read the water level at eye height, and induct[3] a zero when the gauge is empty. Volunteer Saira Bell discovered that a leaning fence post had tilted her gauge, so she moved it to a level platform and documented the change.[4] The correction allowed later readings from her site to be compared consistently.

The network's usefulness extends beyond the morning measurements.[5] Garden groups use the summaries to plan watering, while drainage crews compare reports after intense storms. By gathering modest observations according to one shared method, residents produce a record that becomes more valuable with every participating block.
